deep.reconstruction:
Title: 'Einige Sätze die ersten Gründe der Geometrie betreffend' (some propositions on the first foundations of geometry). This is an attempt on the theory of parallels that takes the equidistant curve as the definition of a parallel. The pencil note 'VIII S.163' at the top refers to Gauss, Werke VIII, p.163, where the page appears to be printed.

(1) Definition. A 'parallel line' to a straight line AB is the line whose perpendiculars dropped onto AB all have the same length. In modern terms this is the equidistant curve (hypercycle) {P : d(P,AB) = h}.

(2) Gauss notes explicitly that whether this parallel line is itself straight 'remains undecided'. In other words, he does not assume the parallel postulate in its equivalent form 'the equidistant is a straight line'. The figure shows the dotted equidistant C-D-F above AB and a straight line A-E rising from A.

(3) Claim. Let AB be straight, CD the equidistant at height AC (AC perpendicular to AB), and AE a straight line making a given angle BAE > 0. Then AE, if extended far enough, meets CD.
- Proof plan: choose n with 2^n > 90°/BAE, so that BAF := 90°/2^n < BAE.
- Take F on the ray AF with AF ≥ 2^n·AC. Then F certainly lies beyond the equidistant, i.e. d(F,AB) > AC.
- Hence the ray AF crosses CD.
- AE lies between AF and the perpendicular AC, so 'a potiori' AE also crosses CD.
- Implicit step (mine): the inequality d(F,AB) ≥ AC when the angle is halved n times and the length doubled n times. It follows inductively from the step 'halving the angle and doubling the segment does not decrease the perpendicular distance'. This is Aristotle's/Proclus' axiom (distance from one side of an angle to points of the other side grows without bound), which is provable in absolute geometry. In Euclidean terms it is 2^n·AC·sin(90°/2^n) ≥ AC. In hyperbolic terms sinh d = sinh(2^n·AC)·sin(90°/2^n) ≥ sinh AC.
- So Prop. 3 is valid in neutral geometry, given that the equidistant is a connected curve separating the strip.

(4) Claim. BE and AC are perpendicular to AB, CD is the equidistant through C, and CE is a straight line. If angle BEC turns out obtuse, then BE < AC, and the straight line CE lies wholly below the equidistant CD.
- Proof: suppose CE (extended beyond E) met CD at F. Drop FG perpendicular to AB.
- AGFC is a Saccheri quadrilateral (GF = AC), so its summit angles are equal: GFE = GFC = ACF.
- In the birectangle BEFG we have BE < GF, so the angle at the shorter side is larger: BEF > GFE. Thus GFE < BEF.
- Missing step (mine): this is contradictory only if ACF (= ACE) ≥ BEF = 180° − BEC, i.e. ACE + BEC ≥ 180°. That holds under Saccheri's obtuse-angle hypothesis, where the quadrilateral ABEC has angle sum > 360°.
- So the passage refutes the case 'BEC obtuse' and ends Q.E.A. (quod est absurdum).

(5) In the remaining supposition (BEC acute), make angle EBH = BEF, alternate angles with respect to transversal BE.
- Then BH does not meet EC (alternate-angle theorem, valid in absolute geometry).
- By Prop. 3, BH does meet the equidistant CT (the continuation of CD on the other side of C). Gauss calls this absurd.
- Implied step (mine): beyond C, on the side of T, the line EC lies between AB and the equidistant. Then BH, starting on AB and crossing the equidistant, would have to cross EC first.
- The aim of the whole page is thus to derive Euclid's parallel theory (straightness of the equidistant, or the angle sum) from the equidistant definition.
errors: Prop. 3 tacitly assumes the equidistant is a continuous curve separating the region near AB from the region beyond it. It also tacitly assumes the doubling/halving distance inequality (Aristotle's axiom), which is not proved on the page. Both are true in absolute geometry, but they are unstated.

Prop. 4: the inference 'BEC obtuse ⇒ BE < AC' and the final contradiction GFE = ACF < BEF need ACE + BEC ≥ 180° (obtuse-angle hypothesis), or some relation between ACE and BEC. This is not stated. As written, GFE < BEF alone is not absurd.

Prop. 5: 'BH meets the parallel CT, which is absurd' requires that line EC, continued past C, stays below the equidistant up to where BH crosses it. In hyperbolic geometry a straight line can stay below or rise back above an equidistant, so this step is unjustified. This is the essential gap: it implicitly reintroduces an assumption equivalent to the parallel postulate.
The machine transcription has letter slips (CF for CD, CD for CE). See the corrections.

results.what: Definition of parallels as equidistant lines, with explicit acknowledgment that their straightness is unproved
results.modern_name: Equidistant curve (hypercycle); 'straightness of the equidistant' as an equivalent of Euclid's fifth postulate
results.usually_credited_to: Posidonius/Proclus, Clavius (1574); critical analysis by Saccheri (1733)

results.what: Any line through A at positive angle to AB meets the equidistant (angle-halving / length-doubling argument)
results.modern_name: Aristotle's axiom (unbounded distance from a side of an angle) applied to the equidistant
results.usually_credited_to: Aristotle/Proclus; proved in absolute geometry (Saccheri, later Hilbert school)

results.what: Refutation of the obtuse case via Saccheri quadrilaterals and birectangle angle-side comparison
results.modern_name: Saccheri–Legendre type argument against the obtuse-angle hypothesis

results.what: Attempted refutation of the acute case using alternate angles and the equidistant
results.modern_name: Failed proof of the parallel postulate (hidden equivalent assumption)
results.usually_credited_to: Many attempted proofs of this kind (Wallis, Saccheri, Legendre, Bolyai senior)

deep.surprise_reason: These are Gauss's early attempts on parallel theory. The annotation 'VIII S.163' shows the page is printed in Gauss's Werke VIII. His occupation with the foundations of geometry (from the 1790s onward) is well documented. The argument is in the Saccheri/Legendre tradition and contains the usual hidden gap.

checkable.asserts: Euclidean case of Prop. 3: at angle 90°/2^n and distance 2^n*AC, the height above AB is at least AC (taking AC = 1).
Hyperbolic case of Prop. 3 (sinh h = sinh L sin θ): with L = 2^n*c and θ = π/2^(n+1), the height is at least c (here c = 1/3).
Identity behind the halving step, 2 sin(x/2) ≥ sin(x) for 0 < x ≤ π/2; the expression simplifies to 0, so sin(x) = 2 sin(x/2) cos(x/2) ≤ 2 sin(x/2).

transcription_corrections: Header pencil annotation: 'VIII S.163' (reference to Gauss Werke VIII p.163); folio number '264' at the top left.
Line 1: 'die [-ab-] Senkrechten' (or 'Perpendikel'); the image shows a word ending in '-kre(c)hten', i.e. 'Senkrechten'.
Prop. 3, cancelled text: '[-AE ≥ 2^n AC so liegt E gewiss schon jens-]'.
Prop. 3: 'so liegt gewiss F jenseits CD' (not 'CF').
Prop. 4: 'falls BEC stumpf ist, wird BE < AC'. The '[?]' word is 'ist' (abbreviated 'st.').
Prop. 4: 'alsdann liegt CE ganz unterhalb CD' (not 'CD ... CD').
Prop. 4: 'Gesetzt CE würde von CD in F geschnitten' (first CD should be CE).
Prop. 5: 'Man mache in dem supposito [-ABH-] EBH = BEF so wird [-B-] BH die EC nicht schneiden, wohl aber die Parallele CT, welches absurd ist'. The figure label '7' at the top left is probably 'T'.
